source_facts: Synthetic computer-vision methods study. In the benchmark setting, all images include both object features and background cues; a supplied cross-background test changes backgrounds while preserving object identity.

Author-provided prior-work summary: baseline B learns from full images; this paper investigates whether restricting feature aggregation to foreground regions reduces background dependence. No exhaustive literature search or priority evidence is supplied.

Method F uses supplied foreground masks during training, but not at inference. B and F share a backbone and train/test split. F scores 81.2% versus B's 83.0% on the original split and 74.5% versus 62.8% on the cross-background split.
There is one training run per method. No object-mask annotation cost analysis or external dataset evaluation was supplied.
request: Draft the final two Introduction paragraphs for a computer-vision methods paper in 140–190 English words. Build a clear technical motivation and contribution around the documented trade-off. Integrate the relevant evidence without turning this into a Results table. Do not assert priority or general superiority; return only the two paragraphs.
rubric: Connect background dependence to training-only foreground aggregation and test-shift trade-off.
Keep original-split performance loss visible; explain contribution without hype or a mere limitation list.
No statistical significance, inference-time mask requirement, or broader validation claims.

variants.text:
When images contain both object features and background cues, performance on an unchanged split leaves open how much a model depends on the background. The baseline considered here, B, learns from full images, leaving both sources of information available. We investigate whether restricting feature aggregation to foreground regions during training reduces background dependence. A cross-background test that changes backgrounds while preserving object identity provides a targeted evaluation of this question, alongside the original split.

We introduce method F, which uses supplied foreground masks during training but requires no masks at inference. F and B share a backbone and train/test split. In this synthetic benchmark, F achieves lower accuracy on the original split than B (81.2% versus 83.0%) but higher accuracy on the cross-background split (74.5% versus 62.8%). This trade-off supports foreground-restricted training as an approach to reducing background dependence under the tested conditions, while showing a cost in original-split accuracy. With one training run per method and no external-dataset evaluation or annotation-cost analysis, the evidence remains limited to this benchmark comparison.

When object features and background cues co-occur in training images, performance on the original split alone cannot establish how well a model preserves object recognition under background changes. The full-image baseline B can aggregate information from both regions, leaving their contributions to prediction unresolved. This motivates a specific question: can restricting feature aggregation to foreground regions during training reduce background dependence, and what performance trade-off does this restriction introduce? A supplied cross-background test, which changes backgrounds while preserving object identity, provides a controlled setting for examining this question.

Here, we investigate method F, which uses supplied foreground masks during training but requires no masks at inference. F and B share a backbone and train/test split. In the available runs, F improves cross-background accuracy from 62.8% to 74.5%, while original-split accuracy falls from 83.0% to 81.2%. This trade-off motivates foreground-restricted training as a candidate approach to background robustness within this synthetic benchmark. With one training run per method, the comparison leaves run-to-run reliability unresolved; external-dataset transfer and mask annotation costs also remain unevaluated.

source_facts: Source Results paragraph: On benchmark D, our method got 42.7 mAP while the baseline got 42.1 mAP. Both were run one time on the same test split. The inference latency on one GPU is 18 ms for ours and 12 ms for the baseline, and the batch size is 1. There are no repeated-seed results, and both models used the same backbone but the baseline used half our training updates. Thus ours is universally superior and its mechanism is proved by the ablation: removing module R gave 42.3 mAP in one run.
request: Rewrite as one precise Results paragraph of 90–130 English words. You may correct unsupported interpretation but preserve every reported measurement and comparison condition. Explain the performance–latency trade-off and the limit on attributing the gain; do not add analyses. Return the paragraph and at most one short author note.
rubric: Preserve 42.7,42.1,42.3 mAP;18 ms,12 ms;batch 1;one run;half training updates.
Do not describe compute-matched comparison or decisive mechanism evidence.
Use coherent result-led writing, not just repeated caveats.

variants.text: On benchmark D, our method achieved 42.7 mean average precision (mAP), compared with 42.1 mAP for the baseline, a difference of 0.6 mAP. Both models were evaluated once on the same test split and used the same backbone. However, the baseline received half as many training updates as our method, limiting attribution of the observed gain to the method itself. Inference latency on one GPU at batch size 1 was 18 ms for our method versus 12 ms for the baseline. The higher observed mAP therefore came with 50% greater inference latency. Removing module R yielded 42.3 mAP in one run, but without repeated-seed results, these comparisons establish neither a reliable performance advantage nor the proposed mechanism.

On benchmark D, our method achieved 42.7 mAP, compared with 42.1 mAP for the baseline, with each model evaluated once on the same test split. At batch size 1, inference latency on one GPU was 18 ms for our method and 12 ms for the baseline, indicating a trade-off between higher observed mAP and slower inference. Both models used the same backbone, but the baseline received half as many training updates, limiting attribution of the gain to the proposed method. Removing module R yielded 42.3 mAP in one run; this ablation does not establish its mechanism. Without repeated-seed results, variability remains unquantified, and these measurements do not support universal superiority.

source_facts: Synthetic cell-biology study. In cell line L, knockdown of protein A reduced marker B by 35% relative to control. Re-expression of A restored B to 92% of control. Both results are from four independent culture preparations; technical wells are not additional biological replicates.
In a second cell line M, knockdown changed B by 3%, with uncertainty including no change. No rescue experiment in M was supplied.
No direct-binding experiment was conducted. The author-provided literature summary says A and B have previously been associated, but does not establish direct regulation or a specific pathway.
request: Write a 130–170-word Discussion paragraph for a cell-biology paper. Synthesize the knockdown/rescue evidence with the discrepant second cell line, explain what the result adds, and distinguish functional evidence from a molecular mechanism. Propose one discriminating next test as a proposal. Do not add citations or merely repeat every number.
rubric: Reconcile cell-line dependence rather than hide or dismiss M.
Rescue supports A-linked B response within L, not direct binding or a universal pathway.
A future test is allowed as a clearly conditional proposal; avoid requiring causal-claim boilerplate despite perturbation.

variants.text: The knockdown and rescue results support a functional contribution of A to maintaining marker B in cell line L, extending the previously reported association between these proteins. Restoration of B towards control levels after A re-expression strengthens attribution of the knockdown phenotype to A depletion. However, the small change in cell line M, with uncertainty encompassing no change, limits generalization across cellular contexts; it does not establish that M is independent of A. Together, these findings suggest that the contribution of A to B depends on cellular context or differences in effective depletion. This functional evidence does not establish direct binding, direct regulation or a specific molecular pathway, because indirect effects remain compatible with the observations. A discriminating next test would compare matched, verified A depletion followed by rescue in both cell lines. Persistence of the discrepancy under equivalent depletion would favour context-dependent function, whereas convergence would implicate differences in perturbation efficacy.

The knockdown and rescue results support a functional contribution of A to maintaining marker B in cell line L: the reduction after A depletion was largely reversed by A re-expression. These findings, obtained from four independent culture preparations, extend the previously reported association between A and B by providing perturbation-based evidence in this cellular context. However, the small change in line M, with uncertainty encompassing no change, limits generalization across cell lines; without rescue data in M, the basis of this discrepancy remains unresolved. The evidence does not establish direct regulation, physical binding, or a specific pathway linking A to B. Indirect effects and differences in cellular context remain plausible explanations. A discriminating next experiment would compare matched degrees of A depletion followed by re-expression in both lines while measuring A and B, testing whether the discrepant responses persist when perturbation strength is comparable. Such persistence would support context dependence over unequal depletion as an explanation.

source_facts: Source paragraph: The treatment made marker Z 1.6-fold of vehicle at 24 h in cell line C. We used three separate cultures and two assay wells from each culture, so n was six independent biological experiments. There was not a direct binding experiment. We conclude drug T directly binds regulator Q to induce Z in every cell type. The culture-level estimate was 1.6-fold with 95% CI 1.1–2.2. The assay-well readings are nested within cultures.
request: Polish this Results paragraph into 75–110 English words. Correct the replication description and unsupported mechanism using the source's explicit design. Keep the marker, time, fold-change and uncertainty; provide one brief note explaining substantive corrections.
rubric: Three independent cultures with two technical wells each, not six independent biological experiments.
No invented statistical method, p value, direct binding or generalization across cell types.
Cohesive, publishable Results prose with brief separate note.

variants.text:
At 24 h, marker Z in cell line C was 1.6-fold that in vehicle-treated cultures (95% confidence interval, 1.1–2.2). This culture-level estimate was based on three separate cultures, each measured in two assay wells. The six assay-well readings were nested within cultures, giving three biological replicates with two technical replicates each. These results support a treatment-associated increase in marker Z in cell line C. No direct binding experiment was performed, so the results do not establish direct binding of drug T to regulator Q or generalisability across cell types.

Note: Biological replication was corrected to n = 3; unsupported claims of direct binding and effects in every cell type were removed.

At 24 h, marker Z in cell line C was 1.6-fold that in the vehicle control (culture-level estimate; 95% CI, 1.1–2.2). The experiment used three separate cultures (biological n = 3), with two assay wells per culture. The six well readings were nested within cultures and therefore did not represent six independent biological experiments. These findings support an increase in marker Z following drug T treatment under the tested conditions. Direct binding to regulator Q was not tested, and the results do not establish an effect in other cell types.

Note: Corrected biological replication to three cultures and removed unsupported claims of direct binding and effects in every cell type.

source_facts: 虚构研究：3家医院的回顾性队列，420名患者；在预先指定的协变量调整后，暴露E与90天再入院的风险比为0.78，95% CI 0.55–1.11。
排除早期事件后的敏感性分析HR为0.96，95% CI 0.68–1.35。未提供随机分配、未测量混杂控制或等效界值。
作者提供的既有研究摘要称不同队列结果并不一致，未提供可验证文献信息。
request: 写一段180–260个汉字的中文讨论正文，形成一个清楚的解释：主要估计、敏感性分析及其对结论的影响；不要把跨1的区间写成证明无效，也不要宣称治疗获益。不新增引用或统计结果，只给正文。
rubric: 中文输出；保留估计方向和不确定性，敏感性分析弱化结论必须可见。
提出合理但非既成事实的解释，不把不同分析直接认定为因果证据。
形成推理而非机械堆叠数值；长度按汉字计，不要求所有数字都复述。

variants.text: 在这项纳入三家医院420名患者的回顾性队列中，经预先指定的协变量调整后，暴露E与90天再入院的HR为0.78（95% CI 0.55–1.11），提示风险可能较低，但区间仍涵盖无关联及风险升高的可能。排除早期事件后，HR接近1（0.96，95% CI 0.68–1.35），表明较低风险的关联对早期事件的纳入较为敏感，削弱了主要估计的稳健性。两项分析均不能确证治疗获益，也不能证明无效或等效；回顾性设计及未测量混杂的可能性进一步限制了因果解释。

在3家医院420名患者的回顾性队列中，预先指定的协变量调整后，暴露E与90天再入院的主要估计为HR 0.78（95% CI 0.55–1.11）。点估计提示较低风险，但区间仍容许风险降低或升高，既不能确立获益，也不证明无效。排除早期事件后，HR为0.96（95% CI 0.68–1.35），提示主要估计对早期事件的纳入较敏感，较低风险的关联缺乏稳健支持。由于未随机分配，且未测量混杂未获控制，现有证据不足以作因果推断；未设等效界值，也不能据此认定暴露E与无暴露等效。

source_facts: Source Abstract conclusion: In a retrospective sample of 620 adults from one hospital, the model prevented deterioration because its internal-test AUROC was 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.93). Calibration was not evaluated. Sensitivity was 0.71 at specificity 0.80. As there was no prospective study, external cohort, or treatment-impact analysis, it is ready for bedside implementation.
request: Rewrite as an abstract Results sentence followed by a Conclusion sentence, totaling 65–100 English words. Preserve all performance estimates, the study setting and untested calibration. Distinguish prediction from clinical benefit and identify the validation boundary without a generic disclaimer.
rubric: Exactly two sentences: Results then Conclusion; retain 620, one hospital, retrospective, AUROC and CI, sensitivity/specificity.
No prevention claim, bedside readiness or calibration claim.
State substantive finding with specific validation gap rather than only warn.

variants.text: In a retrospective sample of 620 adults from one hospital, the model predicted deterioration with an internal-test AUROC of 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.93) and sensitivity of 0.71 at specificity of 0.80; calibration was not evaluated. These findings establish discrimination within the internal test sample, but without prospective evaluation, an external cohort or treatment-impact analysis, they do not establish generalisability, prevention of deterioration or readiness for bedside implementation.

Results: In a retrospective sample of 620 adults from one hospital, the model achieved an internal-test AUROC of 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.93), with sensitivity of 0.71 at specificity of 0.80; calibration was not evaluated.

Conclusion: These findings support discrimination within the internal test sample, but do not establish that the model prevents deterioration or is ready for bedside implementation, because no prospective study, external cohort, or treatment-impact analysis assessed its performance beyond this setting or its effect on clinical outcomes.

source_facts: Synthetic thermal-device paper: a coupled finite-element model predicts 12 W output at 300 K for geometry G and an ideal interface, compared with 10 W for reference geometry H under the same model assumptions.
For geometry G, introducing the measured contact resistance into the model lowers predicted output to 9 W. The 10 W reference was not re-evaluated with that contact resistance.
A prototype of G was measured at 8.7 W at 300 K. One prototype was tested; no repeatability estimates or other operating temperatures are supplied.
request: Draft an unstructured 110–150-word engineering abstract. Explain the design question, connect the idealized model, resistance sensitivity and prototype result, and end with a bounded contribution. Do not assert a measured advantage over H or generalize beyond tested temperature.
rubric: Differentiate predicted 12/10/9 W and measured 8.7 W at 300 K.
No 8.7-vs-10 measured comparison or claim that contact resistance explains every mismatch.
A coherent model-to-device argument, not a catalog of caveats.

variants.text: Thermal-device geometry must be assessed together with interface losses to determine whether idealized performance gains remain plausible in a prototype. We examine this design question for geometry G using a coupled finite-element model and a prototype measurement at 300 K. With an ideal interface, the model predicts 12 W for G, compared with 10 W for reference geometry H under the same assumptions. Incorporating measured contact resistance lowers the prediction for G to 9 W, showing the sensitivity of its predicted output to interface losses. A single prototype of G produces 8.7 W at 300 K. Because H was not re-evaluated with contact resistance, these results do not establish an advantage under matched interface conditions. The study provides a model-to-prototype assessment of G at 300 K, with repeatability and performance at other temperatures unresolved.

This study examines how geometry and interface resistance affect predicted thermal-device output at 300 K and how the predictions compare with prototype performance. A coupled finite-element model predicted 12 W for geometry G with an ideal interface, compared with 10 W for reference geometry H under the same assumptions. Incorporating measured contact resistance reduced the prediction for G to 9 W, highlighting the sensitivity of its idealized performance to interface conditions. Because H was not re-evaluated with that resistance, the adjusted predictions do not establish a comparative advantage. A single prototype of G produced 8.7 W at 300 K; repeatability and performance at other temperatures remain uncharacterized. These results connect interface-sensitive modelling with a prototype measurement at one temperature, supporting explicit treatment of contact resistance when assessing the design.
